metadata.title: Are the New Millennium Learners Making the Grade? Technology Use and Educational Performance in PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The report uses PISA 2006 microdata with a two-stage sampling design (schools, then students). It applies PISA’s complex survey variance estimation via Fay’s Balanced Repeated Replication (80 replicates with Fay coefficient 0.5), which is consistent with using PISA student final weights in estimation and replicate weights for standard errors. For the ICT profile analyses, the methodological annex states that a final student weight (W_FSTUWT) and repeated measures are used in all analyses (except for developing composite indices), and replication methods are used when calculating average scores on indices. The report does not describe any deliberate omission of weights; therefore, analyses should be interpreted as survey-weighted with replicate-based uncertainty, and results are not simple unweighted descriptive statistics.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report explicitly describes plausible values (PISA reports five PVs and the regression is run across PVs with unbiased estimates combined), but it does not provide a corresponding, explicit missing-data handling rule for student-level covariates or outcomes. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain missingness in background variables and ICT items, and the analysis would need to specify whether cases were excluded or imputed. Without this, the exact impact of missingness on the reported associations cannot be fully assessed.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report uses PISA 2006 for 15-year-olds in 57 participating countries/economies, with analyses of ICT access and use based on the subset of countries that administered the PISA 2006 ICT familiarity questionnaire and/or the ICT-related school/principal questionnaire. For the ICT familiarity questionnaire, the report notes it was completed by 25 OECD countries and 14 partner countries (i.e., analyses of ICT familiarity and related confidence measures are restricted to those countries). For the econometric ICT-use impact analyses on science performance, the report states the same statistical model is used for 33 countries (23 OECD and 10 partner) that filled out the ICT survey, implying further restriction to countries with ICT module data. No explicit student-level inclusion/exclusion rule (e.g., complete-case vs imputed covariates) is provided in the excerpt.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes PISA 2006 (15-year-olds) to describe ICT access and use and to examine associations between ICT use and science performance. It uses PISA’s complex survey design and replication-based variance estimation (Fay’s Balanced Repeated Replication with 80 replicates) and applies plausible values for science outcomes by running the regression across five PVs and combining estimates. The report finds that computer familiarity and experience are positively related to science performance, even after accounting for socioeconomic background (ESCS), and that frequency of computer use at home shows a clearer relationship with science scores than frequency of use at school. It also reports that the benefits of ICT use are not uniform: effects vary by students’ economic/cultural/social capital and by confidence in performing ICT tasks. Methodologically, the report emphasizes that the observed relationships do not establish causality and that missing-data handling for covariates is not fully specified in the provided text.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD/PISA technical analysis report rather than an ML predictive study. The schema’s ML-specific fields (ml_techniques, main_findings as ML target-variable rows, and confounders as conceptual predictors for ML models) are therefore intentionally left empty because the excerpt describes econometric/association analyses and descriptive profile construction rather than training/evaluating machine-learning models. Additionally, the excerpt does not provide a single, clearly defined student-level analytic sample size (total N) or per-country N for the ICT module subset, so total_students and n_students remain unavailable.
